chunks: And that which was narrated is: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Bint Ilyas from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I heard him saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by Ruwaythah while he was performing Hajj. A woman stood before him with a young boy of hers and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is Hajj performed on behalf of one like this?' He said: 'Yes, and you will have its reward.'

So there is nothing in it that contradicts what we mentioned, because he (peace be upon him and his family) only said 'Hajj is performed on his behalf' in the manner of recommendation and preference, not that what he said was obligatory. And we have previously established that the existence of wealth, provisions, and a mount are conditions for the obligation of Hajj. So whoever has no wealth and some of his brothers perform Hajj on his behalf, it suffices for him as the Hajj of Islam. That which indicates this is what was narrated:

key_terms.أَجْرُهُ: Its reward (referring to the spiritual reward of the Hajj)
key_terms.الرَّاحِلَةِ: Mount/Beast of burden (one of the conditions for Hajj obligation)
key_terms.الزَّادِ: Provisions/Supplies (one of the conditions for Hajj obligation)
key_terms.النَّدْبِ: Preference/Encouragement (synonymous with istihbab in this context)
key_terms.حَجَّةُ الْإِسْلَامِ: The Hajj of Islam (the specific obligatory pilgrimage)
key_terms.يُحَجُّ: Hajj is performed (passive verb indicating the act of pilgrimage)

ai.seo_question: Is Hajj obligatory for a young child who lacks wealth, or can it be performed on their behalf?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the juristic distinction between the obligation of Hajj (fard) and its recommended performance (mustahabb) for those lacking the requisite wealth or provisions, such as young children. The commentary clarifies that while the child is not personally bound by the pillars of Hajj due to age or lack of means, a proxy’s performance still yields spiritual reward, reinforcing the Shia view that financial capacity is a condition for obligation rather than validity.
